title: Remaining silently changes unit from bytes to megabytes
rationale: Remaining's contract changes from bytes to whole megabytes, so any existing caller that compares its result against a byte-sized limit or file size now gets a value 1 MiB times smaller and will accept uploads that exceed the quota. The integer division also truncates toward zero, so an over-quota tenant with negative remaining reports 0 MB instead of a negative value, hiding the overshoot from the dashboard.

title: Guard does not reject negative limits, which SQLite treats as unbounded
rationale: SQLite treats a negative LIMIT as 'no upper bound on rows returned', so fetch_orders(conn, 0, -1) returns the entire orders table — the exact outcome the new docstring claims this guard prevents. The check validates only the upper side of the limit domain, so a caller whose limit comes from arithmetic that can go negative silently gets the whole table.

title: Lookup breaks its sentinel-error contract
rationale: The change makes Lookup stop returning ErrNotFound, but the callers that would compare against it via errors.Is are not shown in the diff. If any caller relies on the sentinel, it will now treat a not-found result as an unexpected error; the impact rests on that unseen usage.

title: MAX_PAGE guard does not reject negative limits, which SQLite treats as unbounded
rationale: SQLite treats a negative LIMIT value as no upper bound, so fetch_orders(conn, 0, -1) returns every row in the table — exactly the unbounded read the new docstring claims this check prevents. The guard needs to reject limit < 0 as well as limit > MAX_PAGE.

title: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, breaking callers that match the sentinel
rationale: Lookup previously returned the ErrNotFound sentinel, and its declared contract (line 8, which still documents ErrNotFound as Lookup's error) promises it. Callers matching with errors.Is or == ErrNotFound will now never match, silently treating not-found as some other error. If sentinel-based matching is no longer wanted, the error should wrap the sentinel (e.g. fmt.Errorf("user %q: %w", id, ErrNotFound)) rather than drop it.

title: Remaining silently changes its return unit from bytes to megabytes
rationale: The method changes its return unit from bytes to whole megabytes while keeping the name and signature; any existing caller that uses the result as a byte count — for example to admit or reject an upload — now over-admits by a factor of 1<<20. The old contract is visible in this diff's removed comment, so the break is to callers this change does not show, which is why this is info rather than error; a byte-returning variant (e.g. RemainingBytes) alongside the dashboard figure would avoid the cost.

title: Negative limit bypasses the MAX_PAGE guard and returns the whole table
rationale: SQLite treats a negative LIMIT as unbounded, so a call like fetch_orders(conn, 0, -1) passes the new check and returns every row — exactly the outcome the docstring says the guard prevents. A negative limit is a plausible accident (e.g. a computed page size that goes below zero), so the check should reject it too.

title: Remaining() changes its return unit from bytes to megabytes while the rest of the API stays in bytes
rationale: Remaining now returns megabytes while New and Record operate in bytes, so any existing caller comparing Remaining() against a byte limit or recording based on its result under-reports by a factor of 2^20. The method name and its position in a byte-denominated API still communicate bytes; only the doc comment was updated.

title: Remaining changes its return unit from bytes to megabytes, breaking the package's byte-based contract
rationale: New and Record are documented in bytes, so any caller of Remaining that uses the result in byte arithmetic — e.g. deciding whether an upload of n bytes fits — now receives a value 2^20 times smaller with no type-level signal of the unit change. Converting to whole megabytes belongs at the display boundary or in a separately named method (e.g. RemainingMB), leaving Remaining in bytes.

title: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, breaking documented error contract
rationale: Lookup previously returned the sentinel ErrNotFound, which callers are told to check with errors.Is. Replacing it with a fresh fmt.Errorf that does not wrap the sentinel makes errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) return false, so a missing user is treated as a different failure by existing callers; the doc comment on ErrNotFound is also now stale.

title: Exported parseDuration now returns seconds instead of milliseconds, a 1000x change to its return contract
rationale: The return unit of an exported function changes by a factor of 1000 for every accepted input, so any caller still written against the old millisecond contract would act on a value 1000x too small. The docstring documents the new unit, but this diff shows no caller being updated, so the consequence rests on the assumption that callers exist outside this diff and were not migrated.

title: Guard admits negative limits, which SQLite treats as unbounded
rationale: The guard only rejects limit > MAX_PAGE, so a negative limit reaches the query. A negative LIMIT in SQLite means no row bound, so fetch_orders(conn, 0, -1) returns the entire table — the exact outcome the guard and its docstring claim to prevent.

title: Exported parseDuration now returns seconds instead of milliseconds
rationale: The return unit of an exported function changed by a factor of 1000 while the signature still returns a bare number, so the type system gives existing callers no signal; any caller still treating the result as milliseconds (for example, passing it to setTimeout) now runs 1000x short. The diff does not show any callers, so this rests on the assumption that callers exist elsewhere and were not updated.

title: Lookup no longer returns ErrNotFound, breaking callers that match the sentinel
rationale: ErrNotFound is exported and documented as the value Lookup returns for a missing id, but the new fmt.Errorf result neither is nor wraps it, so errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) and == comparisons now fail. Callers using the sentinel to distinguish a missing user from a real error silently take the generic-error path.

title: Guard also rejects limit=0, which SQLite handles safely
rationale: SQLite treats only a negative LIMIT as unlimited; LIMIT 0 returns no rows, so a caller that passed 0 to fetch an empty page previously got [] and now gets ValueError. The docstring's whole-table rationale holds only for negative limits, so the rejection of 0 rests on an inaccurate premise — worth keeping only if a zero-size page is intended to be a caller error.
